claims.text: The target materials are multicomponent metallic HEAs containing 5–8 elements and having homogeneous microstructures.
The proposed reference is a deep-neural-network MLIP trained on ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots.
The training set will span approximately 0.9Tm to Tm and include both high-temperature solid and liquid configurations.
The trained MLIP will replace the EAM reference in thermodynamic integration between the reference and ab initio models.
For the proposed HEAs, temperatures of roughly 1500–2100 K cover conditions at or near melting.
An MLIP trained on diverse high-temperature configurations will capture local energetic variations across both solid and disordered-liquid configurations.
Capturing those energetic variations will make the interpolation between the MLIP reference and ab initio target phase spaces smoother and more representative.
Training on broad high-temperature sampling, including liquid configurations, will produce an energetic landscape that more closely matches the ab initio target.
A closer match between the reference and ab initio energetic landscapes will reduce abrupt free-energy changes along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Conventional EAM potentials are less flexible than the proposed MLIP in representing diverse high-temperature configurations.
Conventional EAM references poorly capture the many configurations in ab initio high-temperature liquids of multicomponent HEAs.
Replacing TOR-TILD's EAM reference with the proposed MLIP will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD using EAM references.
The mismatch error may be reduced by approximately 50% relative to the EAM-reference method.
The intervention is applicable to multicomponent metallic HEAs at approximately 0.9Tm to Tm.
Its applicability to very-low-melting systems, extremely high pressures, and nonmetallic systems has not been established.
Prior successes in elemental and binary systems provide supporting evidence for the proposed MLIP approach.
Scalability and quantitative performance in complex multicomponent HEAs remain uncertain pending benchmarking.

The hypothesis is to be rejected if the MLIP method fails to improve phase-space overlap or fails to achieve a statistically significant mismatch-error reduction of about 50% relative to the EAM control and ab initio benchmark.
